interviewQuestions.question: How do you detect a cycle in an undirected graph, and why doesn't the same technique work for a directed graph?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
For an undirected graph, I run DFS tracking each node's parent (the node I arrived from). When I hit a neighbor that's already visited, I check whether it's my parent — if it is, that's just the edge I came in on doubling back, since undirected edges are stored both ways; not a cycle. If the visited neighbor is anything other than my parent, that's a genuine second path back to a node I've already seen — a real cycle.

This specific trick doesn't transfer to directed graphs, because directed edges don't double back the way undirected ones do — a directed edge u→v doesn't imply v→u exists, so there's no "came-from" edge to filter out. Worse, a plain "has this node been visited anywhere" check (without the parent distinction) is actually too strict for directed graphs: a DAG can have a node reachable via two entirely separate, non-overlapping paths, and revisiting it from the second path is completely legitimate, not a cycle.

What directed cycle detection actually needs is a way to distinguish "this node is still in progress on my current path" from "this node was visited and fully finished on some earlier, unrelated branch" — which is exactly what the three-color (white/gray/black) method tracks, and which I'd bring up as the correct next step if asked to extend to directed graphs.

**Testing:** whether you understand *why* the parent trick is specific to undirected graphs, not just that two different algorithms exist.

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through the three-color method for directed cycle detection, and explain what a back edge versus a cross edge means.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Every node gets one of three states: white (never visited), gray (currently on the DFS recursion stack — in progress), black (fully explored, including every descendant). A node turns gray the moment DFS enters it and only turns black once DFS is completely done with it and everything reachable from it.

During the scan, when I look at an edge to some neighbor, its color tells me exactly what kind of edge it is. A **back edge** — an edge to a currently gray node — means that gray node is somewhere on my current path, and I can walk from it back to itself through the edges I've followed; that's precisely a cycle. A **cross edge** — an edge to an already-black node — means I've reached a completely different, already-finished part of the graph; it's a legitimate shape in a DAG and not a cycle at all.

The reason this works where a plain visited-check fails: gray specifically captures "in progress, on my current path," which is the only condition that actually implies a cycle. Black captures "done, unrelated," which a naive check would incorrectly conflate with gray, producing false positives on any graph where a node has two independent incoming paths — an extremely common, entirely valid DAG shape.

Concretely, I'd implement this as a color array alongside the recursion, returning true the instant a gray neighbor is encountered, and flipping a node to black only on function exit after all its neighbors are processed.

**Testing:** whether you can precisely explain what distinguishes a back edge from a cross edge, which is the actual insight, not just that you can recite "use three colors."

interviewQuestions.question: You need to check for cycles in an undirected graph. Would you use DFS with parent-tracking, or Union-Find?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It depends on whether the graph is fully known upfront or being built incrementally, the same offline-versus-online distinction that shows up across this whole group of topics.

If the whole graph is available before I need an answer — a one-time "does this graph have a cycle" check — parent-tracking DFS is simple, requires no extra data structure, and runs in O(V+E). I'd default to it for a single check.

If edges are arriving over time (say, incrementally adding connections and needing to know the instant a cycle forms, or interleaving cycle checks with additions), Union-Find is the better fit: a "same set?" check before each union answers "would this edge close a cycle" in near-O(1) amortized time, without re-running a full traversal after every addition. Rebuilding and re-running DFS after each edge would cost O(V+E) per edge, which adds up fast if edges arrive frequently.

One thing worth flagging either way: Union-Find only detects cycles in **undirected** graphs — it has no notion of edge direction, so it can't distinguish a directed back edge from a directed cross edge. For directed cycle detection, I'd reach for the three-color DFS method or a topological-sort-based check (Kahn's algorithm with leftover nodes signaling a cycle) regardless of whether edges arrive incrementally, since Union-Find simply isn't the right tool there.

**Testing:** whether you know Union-Find's cycle-detection use is scoped to undirected graphs specifically, and can articulate the offline/online trade-off rather than picking one tool by default.

interviewQuestions.question: A build system's dependency graph is directed, and your topological-sort-based build step occasionally hangs in production with no error, only on certain codebases. How would you debug this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A hang with no error in a topological-sort-based build step is a strong signal that the dependency graph has a cycle that isn't being explicitly detected and reported — if the build code assumes a DAG and doesn't check for leftover nodes after Kahn's algorithm (or a gray-node check in a DFS-based sort), a cycle can cause an infinite wait or a stuck state rather than a clean failure.

I'd first add explicit cycle detection as a pre-check before the actual build ordering runs, using whichever method fits: if using Kahn's algorithm, after processing all zero-in-degree nodes, any remaining nodes with nonzero in-degree are exactly the cycle — log them by name so the failure is actionable ("module A depends on B depends on C depends on A") rather than a silent hang. If using DFS-based topological sort, the three-color method's gray-node detection gives the same information, and the current recursion stack at the point of detection *is* the cycle path.

Once I have that, I'd reproduce the specific production codebase's dependency graph in isolation and run the cycle check standalone to confirm and name the actual cyclic dependency — likely a symptom of a recent refactor introducing a circular import or circular build-target dependency that wasn't caught by code review.

Longer term, I'd make this a hard, fast-failing check at build-graph-construction time rather than something that only surfaces as a hang deep in the scheduling logic — the cost of an explicit cycle check upfront is trivial compared to a hung production build with no diagnostic signal.

**Testing:** whether you can connect the abstract 'leftover nodes mean a cycle' fact to a concrete production symptom (a silent hang) and propose an actionable fix, not just recite the cycle-detection algorithm in isolation.
